trick: Three accounts, three rules. Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Identify the type first and the rule follows automatically.

chapter: Recording of Transactions: Journal and Ledger
trick: The journal is the diary and the ledger is the filing cabinet. Every transaction is written once in date order in the journal, then sorted into its own account in the ledger. Journalise first, post second — never the other way round.

data.prompt: Journalise a transaction, one step at a time.
data.problem: Furniture worth ₹20,000 is bought for cash. Pass the journal entry.

steps.why: Furniture is an asset coming in and cash is an asset going out. Note it is not Purchases: that account is only for goods bought to resell.

steps.ask: Both are real accounts. Which is debited?
steps.why: For real accounts the rule is debit what comes in, credit what goes out. The furniture comes in, so it is debited.

options: Furniture A/c Dr ₹20,000; To Cash A/c ₹20,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹20,000; To Furniture A/c ₹20,000
steps.why: Furniture is debited and cash credited. The total of debits equals the total of credits, as it must in every entry.

data.answer: Furniture A/c ......... Dr ₹20,000, To Cash A/c ₹20,000 — being furniture purchased for cash.

trick: Subsidiary books exist because writing every credit sale in the journal would be unbearable. Each book takes one repeated kind of transaction. And remember the cash book is both a journal and a ledger account at once, which is why it needs no separate ledger posting.

trick: A trial balance that agrees does not prove the books are right. An entry posted to the wrong account, or omitted altogether, leaves both sides equal and the error invisible. It proves arithmetical accuracy only, and examiners ask exactly that.

video.query: trial balance preparation errors class 11 accountancy

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about the trial balance.

items.statement: An agreed trial balance proves that the accounts contain no errors.
items.why: It proves arithmetical accuracy only. Errors of omission, of principle and compensating errors all leave it in agreement.

items.statement: All assets and expenses normally carry debit balances.
items.why: And liabilities, capital and incomes carry credit balances. That pairing is what makes the two columns agree.

items.statement: If a transaction is completely omitted, the trial balance will not agree.
items.why: Omitting the whole entry removes an equal debit and credit, so both sides fall by the same amount and it still agrees.

items.statement: The trial balance is prepared before the final accounts.
items.why: It is the bridge between the ledger and the trading, profit and loss account and balance sheet.

items.statement: Purchases Return appears on the credit side of the trial balance.
items.why: It reduces purchases, so its balance is a credit. Sales Return, by the same logic, is a debit.

trick: Straight line spreads the cost evenly; written down value charges more in the early years. So under the diminishing balance method the depreciation amount falls every year while the rate stays the same — that is the distinction most questions turn on.

video.query: depreciation straight line written down value method class 11 accountancy

data.prompt: Compare the two methods, one step at a time.
data.problem: A machine costs ₹1,00,000 with a scrap value of ₹10,000 and a life of 9 years. Find the annual depreciation under the straight line method, then find the first two years' depreciation at 10% under the written down value method.

steps.ask: Straight line: what is the amount to be written off in total?
steps.why: Cost minus scrap value, that is 1,00,000 − 10,000 = ₹90,000. Forgetting to deduct the scrap value is the standard error.

steps.ask: So the annual straight line depreciation is
steps.why: ₹90,000 ÷ 9 years = ₹10,000 a year, the same every year.

steps.ask: Written down value at 10%: what is the first year's charge?
steps.why: 10% of the full cost of ₹1,00,000 is ₹10,000. In the first year both methods happen to agree here.
The book value is now ₹90,000, and 10% of that is ₹9,000. The rate stays at 10% but the amount falls each year — that is the whole difference between the two methods.

data.answer: Straight line: ₹10,000 every year. Written down value: ₹10,000 then ₹9,000, falling each year.
